property_summary: For every caller address, calling initialize(...) on the correct contract always sets the UUPSInitialized context (so initialize succeeds under onlyInitializing rules including setting the initializing flag for UUPS), whereas the mutant that omits __UUPSUpgradeable_init() fails initialization for some inputs (e.g., when called in a context that requires UUPS initialization), observable as a difference in whether initialize completes successfully (does not revert).

For any caller and accessControl address, calling initialize(...) on the correct contract always succeeds (does not revert) when called on a fresh proxy/implementation instance, whereas the mutant that omits __UUPSUpgradeable_init() can make initialize revert in some admissible call contexts — we assert that initialize does not revert for any caller/address on a fresh instance.

For any caller and any _accessControl address, calling initialize(...) on a fresh C instance always succeeds (does not revert) because the reference calls __UUPSUpgradeable_init() which sets internal UUPS initialization context; the mutant omitting __UUPSUpgradeable_init() can cause initialize to revert when the caller is a contract that performs a delegatecall/proxy-like detection during initialization, so the mutant fails (reverts) for some adversarial caller addresses.

For any caller address and accessControl address, calling initialize(...) on a freshly deployed implementation contract C (not via a proxy) must always complete without reverting because the reference calls __UUPSUpgradeable_init() which sets up UUPS's non-delegated context; the mutant that omits __UUPSUpgradeable_init() can cause initialize to revert when the caller is a contract that makes the call via a proxy-like delegatecall context (i.e. where address(this).code.length == 0 in initializer flow), so there exist fuzzed caller addresses that make the mutant's initialize revert while the reference never reverts.

For any caller address and accessControl address, calling initialize(...) on a fresh C implementation instance when called directly (not via a proxy) MUST always succeed (not revert) because the reference performs UUPS initializer side-effects; the mutant that omits __UUPSUpgradeable_init() will cause initialize to revert when the call context simulates a proxy-like call (address(this).code.length == 0) — we detect this by having an adversarial contract perform delegatecall to C.initialize, which should succeed on the reference but may revert on the mutant.

After calling initialize(...) successfully, the contract's Initializable storage _getInitializedVersion() returns 1 for every input; the mutant that omits setting _initialized to 1 leaves the initialized version != 1 for some inputs (so the property fails).

For any caller address, calling initialize(address) on a fresh C instance always sets the contract's initialized version to 1 (i.e. subsequent initializer cannot be called again) — the mutant that omits writing _initialized = 1 leaves the contract still initializable, so a second initialize call will succeed there but must revert on the correct contract.

After a successful initialize(...) call on a fresh C, the contract must mark itself initialized so that calling initialize(...) a second time reverts; the mutant that omits setting _initialized = 1 allows a second initialize(...) to succeed for some fuzzed _accessControl addresses.

For any address _accessControl, calling initialize(_accessControl) on a fresh C instance always emits the Initialized(1) event (i.e. initializer sets initialized and emits) — the mutant that omits setting the initialized flag still emits the event but leaves the contract in a state where a subsequent reinitializer(reinitializer version semantics) or proxiable check can behave differently; specifically, we assert that after initialize returns, proxiableUUID() called non-delegatedly (direct call) still returns the expected ERC1967 implementation slot and the contract remains non-delegated (proxiableUUID is callable only when not delegated) — the mutant allowing initialize to leave state uninitialized can allow proxiableUUID to be callable in an unexpected context causing differing behavior, so the rule is that proxiableUUID() must be callable and return ERC1967Utils.IMPLEMENTATION_SLOT after initialize for all _accessControl addresses.

After calling initialize(_accessControl) once on a fresh C, the contract must disallow a second direct initialize call (i.e. the second call must revert); the mutant that fails to set _initialized to 1 leaves the contract still initializable so a second initialize call can succeed for some fuzzed _accessControl values.

For any vault/_asset and any prior stored utilization index/lastUpdate, when rate() computes utilization from (index - previousIndex) over elapsed time the reference contract produces a utilization value that, when passed to _applySlopes via rate(), is consistent with the reference arithmetic (i.e., scaling is not applied before division); the mutant that scales before dividing will for some inputs (where (index - prevIndex) is not divisible by elapsed) produce a different returned latestAnswer, so there exists fuzz inputs making the mutant return a different value while the reference returns the canonical one.

For any vault and asset and any stored utilization index/lastUpdate, C.rate returns the same latestAnswer as computed using integer division of (index - prevIndex) / elapsed (i.e., no extra pre-scaling) — the mutant that pre-scales (index - prevIndex) * 1e27 / elapsed can produce a different latestAnswer when (index - prevIndex) is not divisible by elapsed.

For any vault/address and prior stored utilization index/lastUpdate, when block time has advanced the reference computes utilization as floor((index - prevIndex) / elapsed) (no pre-scaling) and returns a consistent latestAnswer; the mutant that pre-scales (index - prevIndex) * 1e27 / elapsed can produce a different latestAnswer for some fuzzed index/prevIndex/elapsed, so there exists inputs where the mutant's rate(...) result differs while the reference's does not.

For any vault, asset and stored utilization data where block.timestamp advances and elapsed > 0, the reference contract computes utilization as floor((index - prevIndex) / elapsed) (no pre-scaling) so calling rate(...) on the reference and then reading a derived observable (the emitted computed latestAnswer via the external call return) will always succeed and produce a value; the mutant that pre-scales (index - prevIndex) * 1e27 / elapsed can change the computed utilization when (index - prevIndex) is not divisible by elapsed, causing rate(...) to return a different latestAnswer for some fuzz inputs — so the general rule is that for all admissible inputs the reference's rate call returns a stable value equal to its internally computed latestAnswer, while the mutant yields a different returned latestAnswer for some fuzzed index/elapsed combinations.

For any vault/asset and any prior stored utilization index and lastUpdate where block.timestamp advances by a positive elapsed, the reference computes utilization as floor((index - prevIndex) / elapsed) (no pre-scaling) and returns a deterministic latestAnswer from rate(...) for all inputs; the mutant that pre-scales (index - prevIndex) * 1e27 / elapsed changes utilization when (index - prevIndex) is not divisible by elapsed, so there exist fuzzed index/elapsed values where the mutant's rate(...) return differs from the reference.

For any call to rate where utilizationData.lastUpdate is zero (so elapsed == block.timestamp), the reference contract uses the vault's reported utilization() to compute the returned rate, whereas the mutant returns a rate computed from utilization == 0; therefore for some vault-reported utilization != 0 the two return values differ.

For any vault/address pair and prior stored utilizationData.index/lastUpdate, when rate() is called and block.timestamp > lastUpdate but elapsed equals block.timestamp (i.e. lastUpdate == 0), the reference contract always uses IVault(_vault).utilization(_asset) to compute the returned rate, while the mutant uses zero instead — so the general rule is: if utilizationData.lastUpdate == 0 then C.rate(...) returns the rate computed from the vault's utilization(); the mutant can return a different value when the vault reports a nonzero utilization.

For any fuzzed inputs, when utilizationData.lastUpdate is nonzero and strictly less than block.timestamp but (block.timestamp - lastUpdate) != block.timestamp, both contracts compute rate from IVault.currentUtilizationIndex and elapsed; the mutant only differs when elapsed == block.timestamp (i.e., lastUpdate == 0) — so we assert that for all inputs where utilizationData.lastUpdate != 0 the two behaviors match (reference satisfies it for all such inputs; the mutant can be distinguished when lastUpdate == 0).

For any vault/address and any fuzzed parameters, if the vault's stored utilizationData.lastUpdate is nonzero (so elapsed != block.timestamp), C.rate(...) computes and returns a value without relying on IVault.utilization when elapsed==block.timestamp; the mutant breaks this by returning a different rate when lastUpdate == 0 (elapsed == block.timestamp) because it uses zero utilization instead of querying the vault — so the rule: for all inputs with utilizationData.lastUpdate != 0, calling rate(...) does not revert and returns a value (both versions produce a value), and in particular the reference never returns the special-case zero-usage value when lastUpdate != 0 while the mutant can be distinguished when lastUpdate == 0 and IVault.utilization(...) != 0.

For any vault/address and any prior stored utilizationData with lastUpdate == 0, C.rate(...) queries IVault.utilization(_asset) and returns a rate consistent with that nonzero utilization; the mutant instead uses zero utilization in that edge-case, so for some vault-reported nonzero utilization the mutant's returned rate differs.

For any inputs, if block.timestamp <= utilizationData.lastUpdate then C.rate returns the same value as calling C.rate after setting IVault.currentUtilizationIndex unchanged (i.e., when no time has advanced the correct contract uses IVault.utilization while the mutant instead computes index delta causing a different returned rate for some inputs).

For every call to c.rate(vault, asset) when block.timestamp > utilization.lastUpdate the contract updates utilizationData.index/lastUpdate and returns a rate computed from IVault.currentUtilizationIndex and/or IVault.utilization consistently; the mutant breaks the rule that when block.timestamp <= lastUpdate the reference reads IVault.utilization() but the mutant instead computes utilization from currentUtilizationIndex causing some inputs to return a different latestAnswer (observable via differing return value), so the general rule: when block.timestamp <= lastUpdate, calling rate must NOT read currentUtilizationIndex to compute utilization — the reference uses IVault.utilization() and thus for all inputs the reference's rate equals the rate obtained when IVault.currentUtilizationIndex is unchanged, whereas the mutant can differ for some inputs.

For every input the reference rejects any SlopeData with kink == 0 (reverting), while the mutant accepts kink == 0 and thus stores it; the test asserts that calling setSlopes with a fuzzed kink==0 leads to a revert on the reference but succeeds on the mutant (so reference always reverts for kink==0).
Reference contract always rejects (reverts) any setSlopes call whose SlopeData.kink == 0, whereas the mutant accepts kink == 0 and therefore succeeds for some inputs (so the stored slopes differ).

For all inputs where SlopeData.kink == 0, the reference contract always reverts setSlopes (rejecting kink==0) while the mutant accepts kink==0 and therefore setSlopes succeeds for some such inputs; thus the reference's setSlopes call always fails for kink==0 but the mutant can succeed.

For every input where SlopeData.kink is nonzero and less than 1e27, calling setSlopes succeeds (no revert); the mutant additionally accepts kink==0, so there exist inputs (kink==0) where the reference reverts but the mutant does not, causing stored slopes to differ.

For all inputs with slope.kink in (0,1e27) setSlopes should succeed (not revert); the mutant wrongly allows kink==0 which changes stored slopes, so the property checks that any nonzero kink either always reverts when invalid or succeeds — specifically we assert that calls with kink >= 1e27 always revert while calls with 0 < kink < 1e27 always succeed, a rule the mutant still respects for <1e27 but only reference additionally rejects kink==0 (so we target existence of kink==0 behaviour by fuzzing and observing revert vs success).

For every nonzero kink value, the reference rejects kink == 0 and also rejects kink >= 1e27 by preventing storage of such invalid slopes; the mutant only rejects kink == 0 and thus will accept and store kink values >= 1e27 — the test fuzzes kink and checks that setSlopes reverts for any kink >= 1e27 (reference reverts) while the mutant would succeed for some such fuzzed inputs.

For all inputs, the reference contract rejects any SlopeData with kink == 0 OR kink >= 1e27 (reverts); the mutant only rejects kink == 0 and will accept and store slopes with kink >= 1e27, so there exist fuzzed kink values >= 1e27 where the reference reverts but the mutant call succeeds.

For every input SlopeData, the reference contract always reverts when _slopes.kink == 0 or _slopes.kink >= 1e27 (i.e., it never accepts/store slopes with kink == 0 or kink >= 1e27); the mutant only reverts for kink == 0 and thus will accept and store slopes with kink >= 1e27, so there exist fuzzed kink values >= 1e27 where the reference call reverts but the mutant succeeds.

For every SlopeData passed to setSlopes, the reference C always reverts when slopes.kink == 0 or slopes.kink >= 1e27; the mutant only reverts when slopes.kink == 0, so there exist fuzzed kink values >= 1e27 where the reference reverts but the mutant call succeeds.

For every SlopeData passed to setSlopes, the reference contract rejects (reverts) any kink that is 0 or >= 1e27, whereas the mutant only rejects kink == 0 and will accept (not revert) some inputs with kink >= 1e27; the test fuzzes kink and asserts that setSlopes reverts whenever kink == 0 or kink >= 1e27 (a property the reference always satisfies but the mutant violates for some fuzzed kinks).

For any supplied SlopeData, calling setSlopes stores the exact SlopeData for that asset (i.e., the getter returns the same kink), but the mutant that removes validation allows forbidden kink values (0 or >=1e27) to be stored and thus diverges for some fuzzed kink inputs.

For every input SlopeData, the reference contract always rejects (reverts) calls to setSlopes when slope.kink == 0 or slope.kink >= 1e27, whereas the mutant (which removed validation) will accept at least one such invalid kink; thus the reference's property is that setSlopes reverts for invalid kink values and the mutant violates that by succeeding for some fuzzed kink.

For every fuzzed SlopeData.kink, the reference contract reverts when kink == 0 or kink >= 1e27, whereas the mutant that removed the validation will not revert for some such invalid kink values (so the property: setSlopes reverts for invalid kink inputs; the mutant accepts at least one).

For all inputs, the reference C reverts when SlopeData.kink is 0 or >= 1e27, but the mutant that removed the validation will accept at least one such invalid kink (i.e., there exist kink values where reference reverts and mutant does not).

For every fuzzed kink value, the reference contract always reverts when kink == 0 or kink >= 1e27 (i.e. setSlopes disallows those kink values), whereas the mutant that removed that validation will accept at least some such invalid kink values — so the property: calls with invalid kink values must revert on the reference but can succeed on the mutant.

For any supplied SlopeData, the reference contract accepts (does not revert) and stores slopes only when kink is strictly between 0 and 1e27 (i.e. 0 < kink < 1e27); the mutant inverts that check and will reject those valid mid-range kinks (or accept only kink == 0 or >=1e27), so there exist fuzzed kink values in (0,1e27) that cause the mutant to behave differently.
